newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's Uralmash plans ADRs end 1997 or 1998.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Uralmash plans ADRs end 1997 or 1998.

text.p: Russian heavy equipment maker AO Uralmash plans to issue level-one American Depositary Receipts by the end of the year or early next year, company president Kakha Bendukidze said on Friday.

He said OAO Uralsky Zavod Tyazhelogo Mashinostroyeniya (Uralmash) would make a private placement of $30-$35 million of new shares which would then be transformed to ADRs, share look-alikes which can trade in the U.S.

"If we hurried we would make the placement in two months and at the end of the year we would have ADRs," he told investors at a CSFB conference. "If there are some delays the placement would be in October and ADRs would be next year."
But Bendukidze did not say that conversion to ADRs was a condition of the placement. "I think that any investor would be happy to do that," he said.
Uralmash, located near Yekaterinburg in the Ural mountains, produces metallurgical, mining, drilling and other heavy equipment.

Uralmash and ZSMK, another equipment maker which mostly produces for the larger company, on May 15 will begin a share swap to form a new entity, Uralmash Industries, which Bendukidze said would cause share dilution.
Uralmash will contribute 90 percent of Uralmash Industries shares and ZSMK will give 10 percent.
A source close to the planned share issue said Uralmash Industries would likely make the issue but details remained to be worked out.
Russia sold 9.32 percent of Uralmash for 41.44 trillion roubles, or 123,338 roubles per share, at an auction on Thursday to Yekaterinburg's TOO Skela.
Uralmash has cut personnel by 33 percent in recent years, decreased energy consumption by 30 percent since 1995 and is spinning off non-core units in a bid to restructure.
Foreign portfolio investors have a 14 percent stake in the company, Uralmash said.

Uralmash 1996 net profit, to Russian accounting standards, fell to $11.1 million after $13.5 million in 1995, though the company did not say whether the basis was cash or accruals. Sales were $170 million in 1996 after $99.4 million in 1995.
But Bendukidze warned that investors should not pay close attention to the Russian accounts figures, which are used to determine tax payments rather than as a management tool.
"Any time you find a company with a huge net profit, you can be sure they have a bad accountant," he said.
He said Uralmash would focus on increased sales and said he expected cash payments, which were 15 percent of 1996 sales, to decrease as it increased sales though barter or counter-trade.
"I do not think we need more profit. We need more sales," he said.
